questions.q: Why can't Northbridge's product-catalog service hardcode checkout's Pod IP address?
options: Pod IPs are encrypted and cannot be read by other Pods
Pod IPs change whenever a Pod is replaced by a crash or rollout, so a hardcoded address breaks
Pods are not assigned IP addresses at all
Kubernetes forbids Pods from communicating directly
questions.explain: Pod IPs are not stable — a replaced Pod gets a new one. A Service exists to provide a stable address that survives Pod churn.

questions.q: How does a Service decide which Pods sit behind it?
options: By a fixed list of Pod names in the Service spec
By a label selector that matches any Pod currently carrying the right labels
By the Pod's creation timestamp
By scanning every node for running containers
questions.explain: A Service uses spec.selector to match Pods by label, and Kubernetes keeps the matching, ready Pod IPs in an Endpoints/EndpointSlice object that updates automatically.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a Service's port and targetPort fields?
options: They must always be identical or the Service fails to create
port is what callers use to reach the Service; targetPort is the port the container actually listens on
targetPort is only used for NodePort Services
port controls encryption and targetPort controls compression
questions.explain: port is the Service's exposed port for callers; targetPort is the container port traffic is forwarded to. They can differ.

questions.q: Northbridge wants checkout reachable from the public internet on a cloud-managed cluster, with the cloud provider handling the external endpoint automatically. Which Service type fits?
options: ClusterIP
NodePort
LoadBalancer
Headless Service
questions.explain: LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to provision a real external load balancer in front of the Service — the right fit for public-facing traffic on a cloud cluster.

questions.q: What role does kube-proxy play for a ClusterIP Service?
options: It builds the container images used by the Service's Pods
It runs on every node and programs routing rules so traffic to the Service's virtual IP reaches a currently healthy backing Pod
It stores the Service's YAML manifest permanently on disk
It replaces the need for a label selector
questions.explain: kube-proxy (or an equivalent data plane) watches Services and Endpoints and programs per-node rules so Service traffic is transparently routed to healthy Pods.
